spans.assertion: the analysis used 146,028 player-referee dyads from four European soccer leagues (2012-2013 season) to test whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players
dyads with missing data and those in the middle skin-tone category were excluded
the final analysis sample included 110,020 dyads, 1,345 players, and 2,851 referees
the adjusted risk difference was found to be 0.18 percentage points (95% CI [-0.02, 0.39], p=0.070), a slightly higher probability of red cards for dark-skinned players
the confidence interval includes zero and the p-value exceeds the conventional 0.05 threshold
the hypothesis is concluded NOT SUPPORTED — evidence is insufficient and the result statistically inconclusive after adjustment
the primary estimand was defined as the adjusted risk-difference in red-card probability comparing dark-skinned (≥0.5) to light-skinned (≤0.25) players
the risk-difference point estimate was 0.1776 percentage points, 95% CI [-0.0151, 0.3902], two-sided p=0.0698
the model adjusted for number of games, player position, league, physical characteristics, and referee-country implicit/explicit bias
the 0.18pp difference corresponds to approximately a 15% relative increase over the 1.22% baseline rate for light-skinned players
since the CI spans zero and p=0.070 exceeds 0.05, the null hypothesis of no difference cannot be rejected
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.1535, 95% CI [0.9864, 1.3488], p=0.0737
odds of a red card were found to be approximately 15% higher for dark-skinned versus light-skinned players after adjustment
the odds-ratio CI includes 1.0 and the result is not statistically significant at α=0.05

spans.note: Model and Estimation Details section header

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad, one observation per pairing aggregated across all matches they met in

sample composition: total N=110,020 dyads; dark-skin subgroup 26,438 dyads (24.0%) with 358 red cards (1.35%); light-skin subgroup 83,582 dyads (76.0%) with 1,016 red cards (1.22%); 1,345 unique players; 2,851 unique referees
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters' assessments of player photos on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.923 with 76.8% perfect agreement
skin tone was dichotomized into light (≤0.25) vs dark (≥0.5), excluding the middle category (0.375) for clearer contrast

adjusted for seven covariates: number of games, player position (12 categories), league country (4 categories), player height, player weight, referee-country mean IAT score, and referee-country mean explicit bias score
the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin-tone ratings
5,609 dyads in the middle skin-tone category (0.26-0.49) were excluded for clearer contrast
8,992 dyads were excluded for missing covariates (position, height, weight, or IAT/explicit bias)
the final analysis sample was 110,020 dyads, 75.3% of the original dataset
the outcome was coded as a binary variable: any red card in the dyad (yes/no)
exposure was coded as binary: dark skin (≥0.5) vs light skin (≤0.25)
categorical variables were dummy-coded, initially without excluding a reference category, then corrected to exclude the first category to avoid perfect collinearity
fit a logistic regression model of red-card probability on the dark-skin indicator, games, height, weight, IAT score, explicit bias, position, and league
used cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) standard errors, clustered by player ID
estimated the risk difference via g-computation: fit the logistic model, predicted red-card probability under counterfactual dark=1 and dark=0 for all dyads, and took the difference in means

performed inference via parametric simulation: drew 10,000 parameter vectors from a multivariate normal (mean=point estimates, variance=cluster-robust covariance), computed the risk difference per draw, took the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles as the 95% CI, and computed a two-sided p-value as 2×min(P(RD≥0),P(RD≤0))
handled missing data via complete-case (listwise deletion) analysis
concluded the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED, including inconclusive/contradictory evidence
characterized the 0.18pp adjusted risk difference as small in absolute terms — less than 2 additional red cards per 1,000 dyads despite a 15% relative increase

characterized the 95% CI as wide relative to the point estimate and including zero, indicating substantial uncertainty consistent with a small protective effect, no effect, or a moderate harmful effect ~3x the point estimate
since p=0.070 exceeds α=0.05, concluded they fail to reject the null hypothesis of no difference by frequentist standards
96.5% of simulations showed a positive risk difference
concluded the magnitude of evidence (p=0.07) is insufficient to definitively support the hypothesis at conventional significance levels
the unadjusted risk difference was 0.138pp versus an adjusted risk difference of 0.178pp
concluded that confounder adjustment slightly increased the estimated effect, suggesting confounders were masking rather than creating the association
concluded the evidence leans in the hypothesized direction but falls short of conventional statistical significance
